similar_scenes.name: Alt-rock de los noventa
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El formato «alt-pop» acuñado por los Pixies (melódico pero no trivial, excéntrico, apasionado sin ser hardcore) continúa en los centros del college-pop: Boston (Belly, Breeders, Letters To Cleo y Morphine, una de las grandes bandas de la década), Georgia (Magnapop), Los Ángeles (Madder Rose), Carolina del Norte (Archers Of Loaf), Nueva York (Dogbowl, King Missile), Holanda (Bettie Serveert), Garbage y Eels. A mediados de década, el epitafio del noise-rock: Poem Rocket, Lynnfield Pioneers, Skeleton Key, Blonde Redhead y el supergrupo Firewater.

artists.name: The Presidents of the United States of America

podcast.title: Birth Year (1976)
podcast.body: The punk explosion in 1976 is widely considered the birth year of Alt Rock, effectively setting in motion the alternative rock revolution. "If we look at the punk explosion in 1976 as the birth year of Alt Rock, 2026, which is when we're doing this, is more or less the 50th anniversary of this music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1

podcast.title: Starting Point (1976)
podcast.body: The year 1976, marked by the "Great Punk Rock Explosion," is considered the starting point for alternative music, influencing practically all of today's alt rock. "Our starting point is 1976, the year of the Great Punk Rock Explosion, the thing from which practically all of today's alternative music emanates."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)

podcast.title: Seismic Years of Transformation (1990-1991)
podcast.body: The years 1990 and 1991 are described as "absolutely crucial" and "every bit as seismic" as the birth and rise of punk in 1976 and 1977 for the history of Alt Rock. This period marked a significant turning point, especially with the explosion of alternative music into the mainstream. "The years 1990 and 1991 are absolutely crucial to the history of Alt Rock. They are every bit as seismic as what we saw with the birth and rise of punk in 1976 and 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alternative Rule (1991-1995)
podcast.body: From mid-1991 through the end of 1995, alternative rock, fueled by grunge at its core and sustained by various other genres, dominated the music scene. This era introduced Generation X to a wide array of subgenres, paralleling the "endless" supply of fresh bands during the New Wave era. "And for the next five years, Alt Rock ruled, spread by the ideals of Lola Palusa and fueled by Grunge at its core and sustained by all kinds of other music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Acceptance (1994)
podcast.body: By 1994, alternative rock had grown so large that it was no longer an "alternative" but had supplanted traditional rock players and become the mainstream itself. This shift, while not immediately problematic, signaled a significant change in the rock music landscape. "Things got so big that by 1994, alternative rock wasn't so much of an alternative anymore. It had supplanted the traditional players in rock and had become the mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Dark Time" After Britpop - 1997
podcast.body: The end of Britpop in 1997 marked the beginning of a "dark time" for Alt Rock, despite many good years in the early 90s, with "rock is dead" cries becoming prevalent. "No one really wanted to admit it in 1997, but after so many good years, it was the beginning of a dark time for Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Decline in 2001
podcast.body: In the summer of 2001, alt-rock was perceived to have "lost its way" after grunge had burned out. Major acts were struggling for direction, and there were too many one-hit wonders, contributing to a general sense of disappointment with the genre. "And alt-rock had kind of lost its way after Grunge burned out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fertile Period 2004-2007
podcast.body: The years between 2004 and 2007 are historically recognized as one of the most productive and successful periods for alt rock. During this time, major labels released strong albums from both established "heritage acts" and promising new artists, while the independent scene grew rapidly in popularity and influence. "The period from 2004 to 2007 has gone down in history as one of the most fertile times for alt rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Disruption Around 2007
podcast.body: Around 2007, alt rock experienced a "rapid disruption" where guitars fell out of favor, pop made a comeback, and an "economic disaster" altered the overall mood of the genre. "The middle arts was a great time for alt rock. Everyone and everything came together at the same time. ... But for the fans of alt rock, it looked like it felt like everything was just fine. In fact, more than fine. But just like we saw in the middle 90s, such bubbles eventually burst as social conditions, economics and demographics continue to inexorably march forward."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Comprehensive History Series (2010)
podcast.body: A 15-part deep dive into the history of alternative rock, titled "the history of alt-rock series," was created in the spring of 2010. This series aimed to examine every facet of alt-rock from its origins in the 1950s up to the contemporary period. "We're going all the way back to this spring of 2010 and a 15-part deep dive into the history of alternative rockets, the history of alt-rock series."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death of the Dance Club Scene (Mid-2000s to 2011)
podcast.body: The Alt Rock dance club scene, which had thrived from the mid-1980s to the early 2000s, experienced a catastrophic collapse by 2011. What was once a right of passage for many clubgoers disappeared almost entirely, attributed to factors like the rise of dating apps, urban gentrification, and a shift in the musical characteristics of alt-rock itself. "By 2011, it was pretty much all gone. A few clubs remained, but the scene was nowhere near what it had been. What used to be a right of passage had disappeared. No more live-to-air broadcasts. It was a catastrophic collapse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: 50th Anniversary (2026)
podcast.body: The year 2026 marks alt rock's 50th anniversary, calculated from its starting point in 1976. "Anyway, that makes 2026, which is when I put this series together, alt rocks 50th anniversary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)

podcast.title: "Golden Age" of Commercial Alt-Rock Radio
podcast.body: The pre-grunge era of commercial alt-rock radio in the 1980s is retrospectively considered by some to be a "golden age." This period was characterized by hardcore music fans staffing stations, who were on a mission to deliver good music, despite low salaries and the constant threat of format changes.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1970s Sound - Guitars by Punks
podcast.body: In the 1970s, the alt rock sound was predominantly characterized by guitars played by punks, emphasizing raw energy and a DIY aesthetic. This guitar-centric approach later evolved with the rise of electronic instruments. "If the alt rock sounds of the 1970s was guitars played by punks"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1980s Culture
podcast.body: In the 1980s, the alt-rock scene, including bands, managers, labels, DJs, record stores, and fans, embraced an "outsider-ness," desiring no connection with the mainstream, and fostered a "very tribal" environment. "People involved in the scene, the bands and the managers, the labels and the DJs, the record stores and fans, reveled in their outsider-ness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1980s Radio Diversity
podcast.body: Commercial alt-rock radio stations in the 1980s exhibited staggering breadth in their playlists, featuring techno pop, industrial, various forms of punk, early rap and hip hop, goth, British indie, remixes, ethereal dream pop, and guitar rock, with each station having a distinct local flavor due to a lack of centralized charts. "This kind of variety was typical for alt rock stations all across North America. No two stations were exactly the same, each had its own local flavor."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1980s Sound - Synthesizers by Punk-Inspired Musicians
podcast.body: By the 1980s, the alt rock sound shifted significantly, becoming defined by synthesizers played by musicians who were inspired by punk. This new wave of artists explored the capabilities of electronic instruments, leading to more radical and diverse sounds. "the alt rock sound of the 1980s was the synthesizer played by people inspired by punks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1990s Boom
podcast.body: In 1991, Nirvana's *Nevermind* sparked an explosion in alt-rock, leading to massive sales for bands like Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Smashing Pumpkins, Stone Temple Pilots, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. This era was driven by Generation X's "insatiable appetite" for the genre, prompting record labels to sign "everyone and anything alternative sounding." "Generation X, the generation driving the culture at the time, had an insatiable appetite for this kind of music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: 1990s Dominance
podcast.body: Alt-rock was the dominant music and culture for about 10 years, particularly throughout the 1990s, during which it fueled the rise of the North American festival scene. "After 10 years of being the dominant sort of music and culture, Alt Rock itself was on the wane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1990s Explosion
podcast.body: The 1990s were characterized by a significant "Alt Rock explosion," marking a period of disruption and popularity for alternative rock music. "Then came the Alt Rock explosion of the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1990s Mainstream Moment
podcast.body: At the dawn of the 1990s, Alt Rock began to experience its mainstream breakthrough, led by grunge, which served as an "entry drug" that opened the door for many other alternative acts over the next five years. "Perfect timing too, because at the dawn of the 90s, Alt Rock was about to have its moment in the sun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1990s Revolution and Fragmentation
podcast.body: The alt-rock revolution successfully kickstarted the 1990s but later fragmented, becoming unfocused and devolving into a series of polarizing sounds by the decade's end. "The alt-rock revolution that kickstarted the 1990s had fractured and become terribly unfocused, devolving into a series of polarizing sounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: 2010s Musical Evolution
podcast.body: In the 2010s, alt-rock underwent a significant transformation, moving "down Temple and away from being guitar heavy." It increasingly incorporated "more keyboards, more samples, more banjos," experiencing a "pop phase more profound than we'd seen since maybe the 1980s." "overall, Alt Rock moved down Temple and away from being guitar heavy, more keyboards, more samples, more banjos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 21st Century Concept Album Proliferation
podcast.body: By the early 21st century, alt rock bands, considered spiritual descendants of the punks, became a primary source of new concept albums, marking a significant resurgence of the format. "And most of them came from alt rock bands, those spiritual descendants from the punks, that killed the concept albums back in the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 80s "Outsider-ness"
podcast.body: In the 1980s, alt-rock was characterized by its "outsider-ness," with participants in the scene, including bands, managers, labels, DJs, record stores, and fans, reveling in their detachment from the mainstream. There was a mutual disinterest between the alt-rock scene and the mainstream.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 90s Resurgence of Powerpop
podcast.body: The 1990s alt-rock scene became a "breeding ground for bands who wanted to explore" the Powerpop sound, leading to a rediscovery of early acts like Big Star. This era saw bands tuning guitars low and turning them up, creating what was essentially pop songs with a grunge aesthetic, or adopting a more "Beatlesque" approach. "As all Rock was on the upswing in the 1990s, most people had their eye on Grunge. But what was Grunge other than Pop Songs with the guitars tuned way low and then turned way up?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 90s Scene for Discovery
podcast.body: The 1990s alt-rock scene is highlighted as an area ripe for rediscovery for those in their mid-40s who loved grunge as teenagers. The scene contained numerous acts, beyond the most popular, that were "adjacent" and went unnoticed at the time, offering "new to you" material with the power and energy of that era.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What A Drag It Is Getting Old (Musically)

podcast.title: Acceptance of Hybrid Sounds
podcast.body: As alternative music grew in popularity, more and more fans were willing to embrace the hybrid of rock and hip-hop, signaling "cool, bring it on!" "As their numbers grew and as alternative music became more and more popular, more and more people were willing to look at this hybrid of rock and hip-hop and go, cool, bring it on!"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alt Rock Revivals
podcast.body: The text references Alt Rock Revivals, specifically mentioning New Wave as the focus of one installment. "This is Alt Rock Revivals Part 5, and this time, the focus is new wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Alt Rock's Mysterious Musicians
podcast.body: The episode focuses on musicians within Alt Rock who have managed to maintain a degree of anonymity, either through disguise and subterfuge or by disappearing from public reach while continuing to release material and maintain a fanbase. "These are Alt Rock's most mysterious musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alt-Rock Shrines
podcast.body: Alt-rock has many sites that have become sacred to its fans, serving as pilgrimage destinations. These locations range from pubs where bands formed to album cover locations and artists' former homes, drawing visitors from around the world. These modern shrines are akin to historical rock and roll landmarks like Buddy Holly's plane crash site or Elvis's Graceland. "There are many dozens of alt rock shrines, but I've picked out my favorites."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Shrines ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: American Alternative Nation
podcast.body: The previous chapter of the Alt Rock history series focused on the rise of grunge and the alternative nation in North America. "The last show was about the rise of grunge and the alternative nation in North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Amorphous Definition
podcast.body: Alternative music was defined by being non-mainstream, ignored by most radio stations, aesthetically "a little left of center," and considered "weird by the majority," qualifying it as alternative by default as there was no other way to categorize it. "If it was a non-mainstream and ignored by most radio stations, b, a little left of center in terms of aesthetics, and c, considered weird by the majority, well then it qualified as alternative by default, simply because there was no other way to categorize it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Billboard Chart Coverage
podcast.body: Billboard magazine features a specialty chart dedicated to alt-rock music, among its couple of dozen specific genre charts. "Billboard magazine. This is where we find the hot 100 singles, the top 200 album charts, and a couple of dozen specialty charts for dance, alt-rock, hip-hop, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music Questions People Almost Never Ask

podcast.title: Birth in the 1970s
podcast.body: The birth of Alt Rock is identified as occurring in the 1970s. "since the birth of Alt Rock back in the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Birth of the Alternative Nation
podcast.body: The concept of the "alternative nation," coined by Perry Farrell, was born around 1991, signifying a growing movement where alternative music gained significant traction and began to challenge mainstream rock. This period marked a rapid shift from niche appeal to a broader cultural phenomenon. "The alternative nation was being born more in a moment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Influence on 90s Alt-Rock Stars
podcast.body: David Bowie was widely acknowledged by the new Alt Rock stars of the 1990s as a major influence, which in turn helped reintroduce his earlier work to a new generation of listeners. "The new Alt Rock stars of the 90s constantly acknowledged Bowie as a major influence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakdown of Prejudices in Early 90s
podcast.body: The alt-rock explosion of the early 1990s was crucial in dismantling many existing prejudices against music created by women, fostering an environment where artists like Tori Amos could achieve success with piano-based music, even amidst the dominance of grunge. "Remember what I said about how the alt-rock explosion of the early 90s broke down a lot of prejudices when it came to music made by women? Well that was one reason."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brief Return to Top 40 (2010s)
podcast.body: In the 2010s, Alt Rock experienced a brief resurgence in the mainstream Top 40 charts, primarily driven by the success of bands like Imagine Dragons and Twenty One Pilots. This was a notable counterpoint to the mainstream dominance of pop, hip hop, and R&B during much of the 2000s. "However, 2X fought against the current and managed to bring Alt Rock back to the top 40 mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 7: (40-31)

podcast.title: Broadening Palette
podcast.body: By the end of the 1980s, the "pallet of Alt Rock just got more and more broad as a new flavor of Alt Rock was born," driven by the influence of punk, funk, rap, hip hop, and metal mixing together. "the pallet of Alt Rock just got more and more broad as a new flavor of Alt Rock was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Alt Rock Explosion (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: The mid-1990s witnessed a significant "huge explosion" of Canadian alt rock, a period during which bands like Barstool Profits secured major label deals. "They were scooped up in that huge explosion of Canadian alt rock that we saw that decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Contribution (Can Rock)
podcast.body: While American Alt Rock was characterized by grunge and punk rock revival, and the UK's by Britpop, Canada's contribution was "Can Rock," a significant surge of new acts throughout the 1990s that continued to grow. "If the main American contributions to Alt Rock were grunge in the punk rock revival, and if the UK's was Britpop, ours was Can Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Embrace of Alt Rock (1990s)
podcast.body: In the 1990s, Canadian Generation Xers enthusiastically adopted both American alternative rock, including grunge, industrial, and punk, and a surge of homegrown Canadian alternative music. By 1995, stores prominently displayed Canadian products, which were highly sought after by consumers. "Canadian generation exers, not only embraced the alt rock that was coming from the States, you know, grunge industrial punk, whatever, but also all the homegrown stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Christmas Song Trend
podcast.body: The annual Christmas show typically features a selection of "weirdo alt-rock Christmas songs from over the decades," which are described as festive songs not suitable for listening with grandmothers. "Usually the annual ongoing history Christmas show features a selection of weirdo alt-rock Christmas songs from over the decades."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Closing Gap with Hip Hop
podcast.body: The new open-mindedness facilitated by grunge music further closed the "attitude gap between alternative rock and hip hop," allowing for greater integration and shared influence. "This had the effect of leading to the attitude gap between alternative rock and hip hop closing even further."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Coalescing Around Generation X
podcast.body: At the start of the 1990s, the Alt Rock scene was "starting to coalesce around the taste of Generation X," with bands like Jane's Addiction and the Pixies gaining notice. "Against this background, the Alt Rock scene is starting to coalesce around the taste of Generation X."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaborative Evolution
podcast.body: The evolution of alternative rock has been a highly collaborative process, incorporating the contributions of a vast number of artists from diverse backgrounds. "The evolution of Alt Rock has been a very collaborative process, incorporating contributions from untold numbers of artists."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Comprehensive History Chapter 12
podcast.body: This specific discussion constitutes Chapter 12 of a complete history of Alt Rock, focusing on Britpop as a counterinsurgency to North American grunge. "This is Chapter 12 of the Complete History of Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Concept Album Stigma
podcast.body: For many years, making a concept album was considered "uncool" within the alternative scene, seen as a throwback to "bloated vanity projects" of the late 1960s and early 1970s. "Now like I said for years, it was considered uncool to make such an album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Consolidation in 1990s Grunge Era
podcast.body: The immense popularity of grunge in the 1990s consolidated and codified alt rock as almost exclusively guitar-based, significantly narrowing its sonic scope. While this allowed the alt rock attitude to explode globally, it also led to the music industry and fans chasing these specific sounds, resulting in dilution and burnout by the decade's end. "Grunge was so big and so popular that it had the effect of consolidating and codifying alt rock as almost exclusively guitar based. The sonic scope of alt rock in the 90s narrowed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Criterion for Influence
podcast.body: For Alt Rock bassists, influence is prioritized over technical prowess. The ability to inspire other kids along the way is considered more important than being the most technically adept on the instrument. "People on this list may not be the most technically adapted their instrument, but they sure is hell inspired to hell of a lot of kids along the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Current State (21st Century)
podcast.body: In the 21st century, alt-rock radio has "loosened up" and "weaned itself at least a little bit from Grunge guitars," experiencing an explosion of indie rock and a greater variety of sounds, though some argue there are now "too few big guitar bands." "Happily, things have loosened up and Indy Rock has exploded. Alt Rock Radio has weaned itself at least a little bit from Grunge guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline in 12-inch Dance Remixes (2010s)
podcast.body: By the 2010s, there was a significant reduction in the creation of 12-inch dance remixes specifically for alt-rock music. While they still existed, they were not produced in the same numbers as in previous decades and were more likely to be co-opted by EDM culture. "There was much less of this music that lended itself to the creation of 12-inch dance remixes, too, which is not to say that they didn't exist. They did, of course. But certainly not in the numbers that we saw back in the 80s, 90s, and early 2000s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: Decline in Interest (2000s)
podcast.body: By 2000, 90s style alt rock experienced a "low in interest," causing bands like The Gufs to break up. This decline suggests a shift in musical trends and audience preferences after the genre's peak popularity. "they were victims of a low in interest in 90s style alt rock, and they broke up in 2000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Decline in Remix Production
podcast.body: The alt-rock genre has experienced a decrease in the number of remixes, a trend attributed to the decline of alt-rock dance clubs after their peak in the late 1990s, suggesting a direct correlation between demand and product. "I don't think we see as many remixes in the alt-rock world as we used to. And I assume that's because after peaking in the late 90s, the number of alt-rock dance clubs went into decline."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Descent from Black Music
podcast.body: Rock and roll, which encompasses alt rock, is substantially descended from various Black Music genres, including the blues, rhythm and blues, jump blues, jazz, and gospel. "It's only right, given that rock and roll is descended substantially from Black Music, the blues, rhythm and blues, jump blues, jazz, gospel, and so many other genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinct Universe
podcast.body: Alternative rock songs are rarely top 40 material, establishing it as a "separate universe in the history of rock music." "On the whole, alternative rock songs were rarely top 40 material. This is a separate universe in the history of rock music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)

podcast.title: Distinction from Mainstream Rock in Late 70s/80s
podcast.body: In the late 1970s and through the 1980s, alt rock and mainstream rock were distinct and separate musical universes, with limited crossover. This period was characterized by a tribal mentality where movement between the two sides was discouraged. "alternative rock and mainstream rock were distinct and separate universes. There was the occasional crossover, but for the most part, mainstream rockers stayed in their lane, and the alt rockers stayed in theirs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diverse Genre Introduction
podcast.body: Through the mainstream success of grunge and grunge-like music, Generation X was exposed to a multitude of genres including industrial, goth, punk-funk, jangle-pop, hardcore, dream-pop, and old folk, broadening their musical horizons. "Through Grunge and Grunge-like music, Gen X at large was introduced to industrial, goth, punk-funk, jangle-pop, hardcore, dream-pop, old folk, and a million other genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diversity of the 1990s Revolution
podcast.body: The Alt-rock revolution of the 1990s was notable for its immense diversity, with sounds being incredibly varied due to the "amorphous" nature of alternative music itself. "One of the great things about the alt-rock revolution of the 1990s was its diversity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant Music Force (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: By the time Depeche Mode reconvened in Madrid in February 1992 to work on their eighth album, Alt Rock had become a globally dominant musical force, with Depeche Mode being recognized as one of the key artists of this era. "By this time, Alt Rock had taken over the world and Depeche Mode was one of the key artists of the era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Introducing "Uncharted": Depeche Mode and the Debauched Devotional Tour

podcast.title: Early 2000s Dire State
podcast.body: At the end of the 1990s and the beginning of the 2000s, the state of alt-rock appeared "pretty dire," although there were some nascent bright spots. "While the state of rock and alt rock looked pretty dire at the end of the 90s in the beginning of the odds, there were some bright spots..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Early 80s Characteristics
podcast.body: In the early 1980s, Alt Rock was largely defined by the use of synthesizers and bands with "fancy names" such as Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and Depeche Mode. The Smiths deliberately set themselves apart from this trend with their plain name and guitar-focused sound. "back in the early 80s, Alt Rock was all about synthesizers played by bands with fancy names like orchestral maneuvers in the dark and de Pesh mode."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: Emergence in the Early 90s
podcast.body: Alt Rock began to assert itself during the time Rivers Cuomo worked at Tower Records on Sunset Boulevard, a period that significantly exposed him to influential bands in this genre. "This was the time when Alt Rock was starting to assert itself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 1

podcast.title: Emphasis on Creativity and Sound
podcast.body: Alt Rock guitarists prioritize technique expressed through creative new sounds, unusual tunings, innovative outboard technologies (pedals and processors), and novel approaches to rhythm and melody construction, moving beyond the classic rock metric of "100 notes a second." "Technique was expressed in other ways other than solos that were measured by speed, you know, a number of notes per second. This leads to a discussion of creativity, you know? New sounds, unusual tunings, different outboard technologies like pedals and processors, new ways of playing rhythm and construction melodies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Classics
podcast.body: Songs like The Smiths' "How Soon Is Now" are now regarded as "one of the great, alt-rock classics of all time," indicating the genre's lasting impact and evolution. "How Soon Is Now. Now, regarded as one of the great, alt-rock classics of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: Evolution in the 1990s
podcast.body: The 1990s were a pivotal decade for the evolution of alt rock, with hip hop's effects driving significant changes in its sound and culture. "how alt rock evolved in the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution in the Early 2000s (The Outs)
podcast.body: After a decade of relative consistency, alt rock began to mutate again in the early 2000s (referred to as "the Outs"). Guitars, while still important, were no longer considered essential, and shifts in attitude and outlook were influenced by major global events. "alt rock began to mutate again. Now, yes, guitars were still important, but not essential."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution through Unusual Voices
podcast.body: The historical evolution of Alt Rock has been profoundly shaped and impacted by the contributions of artists with unusual and distinctive voices, demonstrating that unconventional vocal styles can significantly influence a genre's development. "unusual and distinctive voices have made an impact on the evolution of all rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolving Definition of Guitar Hero (Post-1990s)
podcast.body: From the early 1990s onward, the definition of an Alt Rock guitar hero shifted from solely speed-based solos to emphasize great technique, creativity (new sounds, unusual tunings, innovative use of effects), distinctive presentation, and a certain mystique. "They're just different, you know? Let's make a list, shall we?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Expanding Appetite Beyond Grunge
podcast.body: After the initial "Grunge Gold Rush," record labels recognized an "appetite for Alt Rock beyond Grunge." This realization prompted them to seek out and sign related musical acts, which ultimately benefited pop punk bands. "it didn't take long for the labels to realize that there was an appetite for Alt Rock beyond Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Explosion and Third Wave Ska
podcast.body: The Alt Rock explosion, alongside grunge, contributed to the massive success of third-wave Ska. "This of course was the time of grunge and the Alt Rock explosion. And this helped third wave SCAT become massive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Family Units in Alt Rock
podcast.body: The discussion specifically explores alternative rock groups built around "substantial family units," meaning bands with more than just two members from the same family, such as two brothers or sisters. "Are there equivalents in the world of Alot Rock? What are the biggest family affairs that John has ever seen?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Focus of Discussion
podcast.body: The discussion on artist self-sabotage explicitly focuses on examples within the Alt Rock world. "But what about in the Alt Rock world? That's what we're going to concern ourselves with today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Focus of Influential Bassist List
podcast.body: The discussion of influential bass players is solely concerned with "alt rock heroes" who achieved notoriety and influence since the punk era of the 1970s. "We're concerned solely with the alt rock heroes who thump their way to notoriety and influence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundation for Indie Rock Revival (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: Old-school early alt rock from the late 1980s served as the direct basis for the Indie Rock Revival of the early 2000s. This earlier form of alternative rock was itself a blend of 1960s garage rock and 1970s punk. "Indie Rock, which really was a refurbished version of the old-school early alt rock of the late 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Foundational Conditions for Rise in 1990s
podcast.body: The emergence of alt-rock in the 1990s was underpinned by several foundational changes. These included the demographic influence of Generation X, vast financial flows in the music industry, the pervasive power of music videos, the accurate sales tracking provided by SoundScan, the adoption of digital recording technology, the widespread use of sampling, the proliferation of personal computers, and the mass adoption of the internet. "Let's review these foundational things that were required for Alt Rock to take off in the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fragmentation in the 2000s
podcast.body: Unlike the 1990s, where grunge held a central position, the "center did not hold" in alt rock during the 2000s. The genre fragmented, with bands trying many different things, much like it had in the 1980s, a process that accelerated towards the end of the decade. "In the 90s, grunge held from the center. In the odds, that center did not hold, and alt rock was off-trying different things again, just like it had, way back in the 80s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Future Resurgence
podcast.body: Despite bottoming out at the end of the 1990s, the seeds for alt-rock's next cycle were already being planted, with a new crop of indie bands like The Arctic Monkeys and Arcade Fire poised to bring it back into the spotlight. "But even as the 90s died out, in alt-rock bottomed out, the seeds for the next cycle were already being planted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Generation Y's Role in Resurgence
podcast.body: The resurgence of alt-rock would be driven by a new generation of artists, arriving in time to ride a new demographic change, suggesting that Generation Y would play a crucial role in its "resurrection." "Rock and alt rock would rise again. And this resurrection would start with a new generation of artists, with new sounds, new attitudes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Golden Age (1980s)
podcast.body: In retrospect, some consider the 1980s to be the "golden age of commercial alt-rock radio" due to the immense musical variety and the passionate, mission-driven staff dedicated to delivering "good music to the masses." "But in retrospect, some consider this to be the golden age of commercial alt-rock radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gorillaz Debut Album Component
podcast.body: Alt-rock was one of the genres that contributed to the experimental sound of the Gorillaz's debut album, alongside trip-hop, Brit-pop, dub, reggae, and hip-hop. "The music was rather experimental, more trip-hop, some alt-rock, bits of Brit-pop, little dub, little reggae, and a bunch of hip-hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge as "Training Wheels"
podcast.body: Grunge served as "Alt Rock with training wheels," successfully luring millions of people into the alternative music scene with its accessible yet distinct approach to traditional guitar rock. This exposure encouraged listeners to explore deeper into alt-rock and other genres, enriching their musical lives.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge's Catalyst for Mainstream Influx
podcast.body: The arrival of Grunge "ripped a hole in the music space-time continuum," creating a "tear into a parallel universe" that allowed a flood of previously evolving alternative sounds and scenes to invade the mainstream. "Then along came Grunge, the biggest sound of the decade. It ripped a hole in the music space-time continuum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Grunge's Impact (1990s)
podcast.body: With the rise of grunge in the early 1990s, particularly bands like Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Alice in Chains, and Nirvana, alt-rock began to "coalesce around hard guitar rock," becoming less diverse and eventually supplanting the mainstream. "Alt Rock began to coalesce around hard guitar rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Harder End Radio Format (2010s)
podcast.body: The 2010s witnessed the rise of a new radio format focused on the harder end of alt rock, largely remaining an American phenomenon with roots in the nu metal era. "The 2010s also saw the rise of a new radio format that focused on the harder end of alt rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Harder End of Dominance
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, Tool's cassette demo tape fit well with the "harder end" of Alt Rock, a genre that was dominating the music scene during that period. "fit nicely with the harder end of Alt Rock that was dominating music in those days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Deep Dive
podcast.body: The history of alt-rock is subject to a 15-part deep dive series, examining every facet from the 1950s up to the present day. "This is the complete history of Alt Rock, chapter 4."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: History in the 2000s
podcast.body: The early 2000s ("the Outs") saw a new generation of young musicians, playing stripped-down rock, rising in popularity through independent labels, constituting a significant chapter in the history of alt rock. "This is the second part of a series of programs on the history of Alte Rock in the Outs, that decade between 2000 and 2009."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Homogenization of Sound (1990s)
podcast.body: Grunge's immense popularity led to the homogenization of alt-rock radio playlists, as program directors across North America began to follow the trends of larger stations like KROQ in Los Angeles, largely squeezing out the varied sounds of the 1980s in favor of big guitars and screaming vocalists. "The result was an unstoppable march towards a homogeneity in sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hope for Electronica as Savior
podcast.body: For a few weeks in the spring of 1997, there were predictions that Alt Rock would be "saved" by Electronica, especially after The Prodigy's album *Fat of the Land* topped charts worldwide, though this ultimately did not materialize. "And for a few weeks in the spring of 1997, there were predictions that All Rock would be saved for this amorphous thing called electronica, especially after the prodigy had a number one album all over the world with Fat of the Land."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hüsker Dü's Contribution
podcast.body: Hüsker Dü's 1984 double album "Zen Arcade" is credited with significantly contributing to the creation of what would eventually be categorized as alternative rock, bridging the gap between hardcore and more accessible music. "Husker Do's greatest indie achievement was a 1984 double album called Zen Arcade, a record that went a long way towards creating what would be categorized as alternative rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Generational Shift
podcast.body: The decline of alt-rock was partly due to a new generation, Generation Y, entering their years of musical awareness, who preferred pop-oriented tastes over brooding grunge or intense post-punk alt-rock. "Generation Y just wasn't into brooding grunge or any of the kind of intense post punk all rock that their forebearers were."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Grunge on Alt-Rock
podcast.body: Grunge effectively "ruined" the diverse nature of 80s alt-rock by causing it to coalesce around hard guitar rock, leading to a homogenization of sound. As record labels and sales surged, the focus shifted predominantly to guitar-based music, marginalizing other varied sounds that were once prominent.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Importance of Presentation and Mystique
podcast.body: An Alt Rock guitar hero needs a unique sense of style and performance, where "how they play is just as important as what they play," combined with an intriguing mystique about their methods, ideas, equipment, and personality. "Now guitar heroes have to have a certain sense of style and performance that's really hard to quantify how they play is just as important as what they play."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Indispensable Development Tool
podcast.body: Despite initial rejection, the concept album has, in a couple of cases, been an indispensable part of the development of the alternative scene itself. "In fact, in a couple of cases, it's been indispensable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence of Lou Reed
podcast.body: The very existence and known form of Alt Rock are questioned without the foundational influence of Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground, underscoring their critical role in shaping the genre. "Where would Alt Rock be today if it hadn't been for Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground? Would it even exist as we know it?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influential Bands
podcast.body: Joy Division is considered one of the most influential bands in the entire history of Alt Rock. New Order also became extremely influential in the history of Alt Rock, albeit in a different style than Joy Division. "The Division is now legendary, one of the most influential bands in the entire history of Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Intensity in Early 1990s
podcast.body: The early 1990s saw intense alt rock emerge, coinciding with the 1990 recession. "The next recession came in 1990, which, as we all know, began grunge and the intense alt rock that we saw early in that decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Intersection with Civil Aviation
podcast.body: The podcast episode explores the various intersections between alt-rock music and civil aviation, covering topics such as air rage incidents involving alt-rock musicians, high-altitude concerts, rock stars who are licensed pilots, plane incidents, and fatal crashes that have impacted the alternative rock community. "Show number 747 will be about civil aviation and alt-rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jimmy Chamberlin's Versatility
podcast.body: Jimmy Chamberlin, known for his work in The Smashing Pumpkins, integrated his background as a swing and big band drummer into his alt-rock playing, bringing a distinctive swing rhythm and intelligent hi-hat use to the genre. "The smashing pumpkins with X-Swing and Big Band drummer Jimmy Chamberlain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

podcast.title: Late 1990s Decline
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, alt-rock began to wane as artists either grew up, moved on, or broke up, and the music fragmented with many one-hit wonders. New artists often seemed derivative, leading to a "Creed Syndrome" where the music felt watered down. "After 10 years of being the dominant sort of music and culture, Alt Rock itself was on the wane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 1990s One-Hit Wonder Trend
podcast.body: The late 1990s witnessed a notable increase in the number of alt rock bands that gained brief prominence with a single hit song before fading from the mainstream. This trend was attributed to the genre's overall exhaustion and lack of direction after the grunge and "alternative nation revolution" of the early part of the decade. "This is when we began to see an inordinate uptick in the number of bands who came and went with just one song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Late 90s Decline and Splintering
podcast.body: By 1997, Alt Rock was struggling to maintain public attention as Gen X aged, the economy improved, and Gen Y ushered in a pop phase. The genre had "splintered into a million different subgenres," resulting in a proliferation of one-hit wonders and a general downturn. "All Rock was definitely struggling to keep the public's attention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza's Original Focus (1990s)
podcast.body: When Lollapalooza was initially conceived in 1990, it was a touring festival primarily focused on "left-of-center and alternative bands" and was an essential part of 90s music culture. "When La La Palosa was first conceived in 1990, it was a full-blown touring festival of Weirdos, featuring the best in left-of-center and alternative bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 4: (70-61)

podcast.title: Long-standing Cycles
podcast.body: Alt Rock has been around long enough to exhibit identifiable cycles of revivals, similar to how Ska keeps making comebacks. "Alt Rock has been around long enough for us to be able to identify certain cycles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Longest-Serving Musician
podcast.body: Lou Reed is identified as the longest surviving alt-rock new rock musician in the world, having maintained a continuous career of recording and touring since 1958. This makes him a significant figure in the genre's history. "he is the longest surviving alt-rock new rock musician in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

podcast.title: Lost Albums Phenomenon
podcast.body: A significant number of albums in Alt Rock are either partially or fully made but never officially released, earning them the moniker of "lost albums." These projects, often involving prominent artists, become the subject of myths due to their elusive nature. "There are a surprising number of lost albums out there, records that were made or at least partially made, that apparently will never, ever see the light of day. And they involve some pretty big names. These are the lost albums of Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Loyal Fanbase
podcast.body: Tool is noted for cultivating "some of the most loyal fans anywhere" within the alt-rock world, demonstrating a deep connection between the band and its audience that has endured through decades. "Tool has some of the most loyal fans anywhere in the alt rock world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Made Possible by Key Bands – Contribution of Chris Cornell's Groups
podcast.body: Alt Rock was significantly influenced and made possible by bands like Soundgarden, which featured Chris Cornell. His contributions and the impact of his groups were crucial to the genre's development and widespread acceptance. "his passing marks the end of one of the band who made Grunge and Alt Rock possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Moshing as Tribal Behavior (1990s)
podcast.body: As alternative rock gained popularity throughout the 1990s, moshing became an ingrained "tribal behavior" for the Alt Rock generation. It evolved from an activity at aggressive hardcore punk shows to an expected practice at almost all alternative rock gigs, regardless of the musical style. "What began as an activity at super aggressive hardcore punk shows started showing up at all Alt Rock gigs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Most Valuable Collectible (Formerly)
podcast.body: The Sex Pistols' "God Save the Queen" 7-inch single, specifically the A&M Records pressing from 1977, was for a long time considered the most valuable alt-rock collectible. This rare single commanded prices around $24,000 at auction due to its history of being ordered destroyed. "The perennial holder of the High Watermark in Alt Rock has been up until recently the Sex Pistols God Save the Queen 7-inch single."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Book of World Records Version 1.0 - Part 2

podcast.title: Mythical Doom Figure
podcast.body: Ian Curtis, singer of Joy Division, became a mythical "doom figure" in Alt Rock following his suicide. "Now Ian has gone on to become a mythical doom figure in Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: North American Appetite
podcast.body: In the early to mid-90s, North America developed a "massive appetite for all things alternative," largely driven by grunge, which subsequently threatened to dominate the global rock music scene. "North America had developed a massive appetite for all things alternative, like by Grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: North American vs. British Scenes
podcast.body: The history of alt-rock in 1990-1991 must be viewed through the lens of developments in both North America and Britain, as distinct forces and movements were shaping the genre on both continents. "And again, we have to divide things between what was happening in North America versus what was going on in Britain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonder Measurement Challenges
podcast.body: The traditional Billboard definition of a one-hit wonder (a single reaching the Top 40) is inadequate for Alt Rock due to its non-mainstream nature, as much of this music never charted in the Top 40, necessitating alternative metrics. "The standard Billboard definition doesn't work because we're dealing with non-mainstream material. Much of this stuff never made it onto the standard top 40 charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1

podcast.title: One-Hit Wonders Phenomenon
podcast.body: The 90s alt-rock boom, characterized by rapid label signings, also produced many "one-hit wonders." Labels would sign bands if they sounded "alternative and halfway decent," and consumers would buy full CDs for just one big hit song, regardless of the album's overall quality. Sometimes labels would bail on promoting subsequent singles after an initial hit, or the band's sound would simply fall out of cultural favor. "But there were some misses along the way. And some of those signings only had one good song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Open-minded Fanbase
podcast.body: Fans of alternative music distinguished themselves by not carrying the "perceptual baggage" that mainstream rock fans had about rap and hip-hop, priding themselves on an open mind and a willingness to try "the newest and weirdest music out there." "One of the cool things about the people who were into alternative music was that they didn't carry some of the same perceptual baggage that mainstream rock fans had about rapping hip-hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Openness to Diverse Expression
podcast.body: Alt Rock has a historical reputation for being receptive to various forms of expression, providing a home for artists with unconventional approaches to music. "And because Alt Rock has a history of being open to, shall we say, different forms of expression, some of these souls have found homes in the province of Rock and Roll."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins and Influential Voices
podcast.body: The evolution of Alt Rock was significantly shaped by artists with unusual and distinctive voices. Key figures like Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground are considered foundational, influencing later generations of musicians by demonstrating the acceptance of "weirdness" and experimentation. "Where would Alt Rock be today if it hadn't been for Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground? Would it even exist as we know it?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins in Garage Bands and Punk
podcast.body: The history of alt rock is said to have begun with garage bands in the late 1960s and was significantly shaped by the punk rock explosion of the mid-1970s. "If you're an alt rock fan, you've heard the story of how this all began with the garage band to the late 60s and the punk rock explosion of the mid 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Palette of Sounds Expansion
podcast.body: By 1995, the range of sounds available to alt rockers had "increased dramatically" due to the influence of hip-hop, extending beyond traditional grunge punk and electronic elements. "the palette of sounds available to alt rockers had increased dramatically beyond just grunge punk in the various electronic sounds that had brought us this far."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Platform for Unique Female Artists
podcast.body: The world of Alt-Rock has provided a space for female artists who sound and look unlike anyone else, often displaying "fantastic and sometimes bewildering senses of style and poise and confidence." These extraordinary artists challenge conventions and bring new richness to music. "But when we slide into the world of alt-rock, there are some women who sound like no one else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pop Side Dominance by Folk-Acoustic
podcast.body: The pop side of alt rock in the 2010s was dominated by folk-y, acoustic guitar, and banjo bands, which seemed to monopolize public attention. "And the pop side of Alt Rock was dominated by Foki, acoustic guitars, and banjo bands, which seem to be taking up all the oxygen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Post-Cobain Vacuum
podcast.body: Following Kurt Cobain's death in 1994, a creative and spiritual vacuum emerged in alt-rock. This void needed to be filled, creating an opportunity for bands like The Offspring and Green Day to rise to prominence. "his death opened up a creative and spiritual vacuum in alt-rock and that vacuum needed to be filled with something."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Aimlessness
podcast.body: After the widespread influence of grunge and the "alternative nation revolution" in the early 1990s, the broader alt rock scene became perceived as "tired and aimless," creating an environment where it was difficult for many bands to sustain long-term commercial success beyond a single breakthrough. "Well, basically the whole scene had grown tired and aimless after grunge and the whole alternative nation revolution that had engulfed the early part of the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Homogeneity on Radio
podcast.body: The immense popularity of grunge led to alt-rock radio stations across North America adopting a more homogeneous sound. Program directors began to mimic playlists from larger stations like K-Rock in Los Angeles, rather than developing local flavors, resulting in a focus on big guitars and screaming vocalists.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Playlisting Conservatism
podcast.body: After the grunge era, commercial alt-rock radio became conservative, preferring to play "grunge or grunge-ish" (guitar-based, often with drop-tuning) music rather than taking chances on genuinely new and different sounds. This approach, driven by a desire for stable ratings and revenues, led to tightened playlists and a diminished variety.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Shift to Guitar-Centric
podcast.body: Grunge decidedly swung Alt Rock towards big guitar bands, making them the most public and accepted face of the genre, though variety still existed below the surface. "Grunge though swung things decidedly in the direction of big guitars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Slump (Late 1990s)
podcast.body: After the initial grunge bands "died off" and the "grunge well basically went dry," the late 1990s experienced a period where "nothing concrete to replace it" emerged, leading to "Dreck-like New Metal" and a grim outlook for the genre. "The original Grunge bands died off and we were left with Dreck-like New Metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-90s Choice Overload
podcast.body: Before the 1990s, those into alternative music were "spoiled for choice" due to the thriving multiple genres, sub-genres, and even sub-sub-sub-sub-sub-sub-genres within the alt-rock universe, ensuring there was something for everyone. "This means that if you were into alternative music before the 1990s, you were spoiled for choice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Grunge Diversity
podcast.body: Before Grunge arrived in force in 1991, ushering in an era of mainly guitar-based music, alt rock was known for an extremely wide range of sounds and textures. "Before Grunge arrived in force in 1991 and ushered in an era of mainly guitar-based music, All Rock was known for an extremely wide range of sounds and textures."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)

podcast.title: Pre-Grunge Diversity
podcast.body: Before the emergence of grunge, Alt Rock encompassed a vast variety of adventurous, different, and sometimes weird sounds, with many different types of artists, including guitar bands, synth-bass groups, singer-songwriters, industrial groups, electronic outfits, and dancey bands. "a vast variety of sounds that were adventurous, different, and sometimes weird."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Grunge Diversity in 80s Radio
podcast.body: In the 1980s, commercial alt-rock radio stations were not connected by industry charts or tracked airplay, leading to a "staggering breadth of music" on playlists. This included techno pop, industrial, various punk styles, early rap/hip pop, Goth, British indie, dance remixes, ethereal dream pop, and a smattering of guitar rock, with no two stations sounding exactly alike.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Predominantly White Perception
podcast.body: Alt-rock, along with rock and indie rock, is widely perceived as predominantly white, sparking discussions about cultural identification and barriers to participation. "Rock, alt, rock and indie rock are predominantly white."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Presence of Piano Heroes
podcast.body: While alt rock is often primarily associated with guitar-driven music, there are indeed "piano heroes" within the genre, though they may be "a bit hard to spot." These artists distinguish themselves by basing their music around the piano, adding unique color and texture to the alt rock sound. "Any piano heroes from the world of Alt Rock? Does even such a thing exist? Well, actually, yes. They're a bit hard to spot, but they're out there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Punk Roots
podcast.body: Understanding the origins of punk rock in the mid-1970s is crucial for comprehending where today's alt-rock came from and for predicting future musical trends, as punk was the "big bang moment" for alternative music. "This you want to know where today's alt rock came from and you're looking to predict what may happen to our music in the future."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radiohead's Place
podcast.body: Radiohead is recognized as one of the most revered, influential, and thoroughly analyzed groups in the entire history of Alt Rock. "Radiohead has become one of the most revered, most influential, and most analyzed groups in the history of Alt Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Resurgence of Variety Post-2000s
podcast.body: In recent times, alt-rock radio has "loosened up" and "weaned itself" from its over-reliance on grunge guitars, leading to an explosion of indie rock. The variety of sounds on alt-rock radio playlists is now much greater than it has been in quite some time, although some argue there are too few big guitar bands today.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Return to 80s Diversity in 2000s
podcast.body: The 2000s (Oughts) brought a return of alt rock to its diverse roots of the 1980s, acknowledging a new generation's more sensitive side. There was less emphasis on being a full-on guitar band in the way alt rock had been defined in the 1990s. "What the odds brought back was a return of alt rock to what it was like back in the 80s. What it did was acknowledge this new generation's more sensitive side."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise in Early 2000s
podcast.body: While initially "invisible" as the calendar turned from 1999 to 2000, indie alt-rock was starting to become "really interesting" and its time for prominence was anticipated, leading into a period of significant growth. "Yes, things were starting to get really interesting with the rise of indie alt-rock, but that was still largely invisible as the calendar moved from 1999 to 2000. It's time would come, but not quite yet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 3: The Return of Rock

podcast.title: Role in Concept Album Decline
podcast.body: Alt Rock, alongside Punk, played a significant role in the disappearance of the concept album in the 1980s and 1990s, viewing such projects as "vestiges of old rock" that needed to be "expunged from the culture." "Punk and Alt Rock had a lot to do with its death because these types of projects were seen as vestiges of old rock and needed to be expunged from the culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shake-up from Cobain's Death
podcast.body: The passing of Kurt Cobain in April 1994 "shook" all of North American alt-rock, leaving musicians uncertain how to react or move on, and creating a decline or "mired in confusion, sadness, and doubt" for American-bred rock. "In fact, all of North American alt-rock was shaken by Kurt's passing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shift Away from Loud Guitars (2010s)
podcast.body: While loud, big guitars were still present, many new alt-rock acts in the 2010s moved in a different direction, favoring acoustic instruments and a less intense sound. "You know, loud big guitars are still there, but so many new acts went in another direction, especially alt rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Shift Towards Less Aggressive Music (2010s)
podcast.body: Much of the alt-rock that made it to radio in the 2010s became less intense, more pop-oriented, less aggressive, and generally more mid-tempo. This shift in musical style contributed to the decline of the alt-rock dance club scene, as the new material was less conducive to high-energy dancing. "much of the alt-rock of the 2010s was less intense and more pop. What made it to the radio was, in general, much less aggressive and beat heavy and much more mid-tempo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 5: Music and Tech

podcast.title: Shift from Alternative to Mainstream
podcast.body: The flood of alt-rock into the mainstream, triggered by Grunge, was so strong that the term "alternative music" eventually lost its original meaning, as "Alternative became mainstream," making it no longer an alternative to anything except the artists it displaced. "This flood was so strong that it wasn't long before the term alternative music lost any meaning. Alternative became mainstream, meaning that it wasn't an alternative to anything really, except the pushed out artists that would now form the basis of a new radio format called Classic Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shifting Audience and Openness
podcast.body: The original post-punk alt-rock audience "had aged," leading to "the older, said in their ways crowd" being replaced by a new generation with "no preconceived notions or baggage" regarding new sounds like rap, which they viewed as exciting new music. "The original post-punk alt-rock audience had aged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Skateboarding Culture Subgenre
podcast.body: There is a whole subgenre of Alt Rock that is built upon skateboarding culture, demonstrating a significant crossover between the music and the sport. "In fact there's a whole subgenre of Alt Rock built on skateboarding culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Songs Inspired by Real Events
podcast.body: Alt-rock songs often delve into true stories, real people, and actual events, forming a historical record that provides deeper context and emotional impact for listeners. "This program is all about the true stories behind big, alt-rock songs, real people, and real events inspired these tracks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sonic Diversity in Late 70s/80s
podcast.body: During the late 1970s and 1980s, the alt rock world encompassed a vast variety of developing sounds, unbound by a specific sound, but rather by an "anything goes" attitude that was left of center, experimental, or disagreeable to mainstream rock. Its sonic palette was very wide, deep, and varied. "the sonic palette of alternative music back in the late 70s and through the 80s was very, very wide, very, very deep and very varied."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Alt Rock Gold Rush (1990s)
podcast.body: The introduction of SoundScan technology in 1991 sparked an "Alt Rock Gold Rush" within the music industry. Once labels had accurate data showing that "weirdo music" like alt-rock was selling massive units without significant marketing, they began to invest heavily in promoting it and signing more talent. This direct link between sales data and label investment fueled the genre's explosive growth. "The Alt Rock Gold Rush was on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Call's Success
podcast.body: The Call experienced success within the Alt Rock world during the 1980s and 90s, releasing nine studio albums. "The call had some success in the Alt Rock world through the 1980s and 90s with nine studio albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tracing Origins from 1950s to Present
podcast.body: The alt-rock series provides a historical overview of the genre, exploring its evolution and various facets from the 1950s, tracing its development right up to modern times. "this series that examines every single facet of alt-rock from the 1950s right up to, well, pretty much today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Chart Performance (2010s)
podcast.body: Alt rock performed "pretty well" in the UK during the 2010s in terms of chart performance, with acts from indie labels showing great success. "Starting with the UK, where Alt Rock did actually pretty well, at least as far as chart performance was concerned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Unexpected Popularity of Grunge (Early 90s)
podcast.body: The sudden popularity of grunge in the early 1990s, a distinct branch of alt-rock, "caught everybody by surprise." Previously, this music was largely considered "music for weirdos and outsiders." "The sudden popularity of this branch of alt-rock caught everybody by surprise. Up until the early 90s, this was music for weirdos and outsiders."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vinyl Adherence (Post-CD Era)
podcast.body: Many alt-rock bands, alongside punk, never fully embraced digital formats, continuing to release 7-inch singles and vinyl albums to independent record stores. "Punk and other alt-rock bands. There were many groups who never bought into digital ever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Weezer's Classification
podcast.body: Weezer is classified within the Alt Rock genre, specifically referred to as "Alt Rock's Nerd Heroes." "This is part two of Rivers Quomo and Weezer, Alt Rock's Nerd Heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 2

podcast.title: World Party's Debut Contributions
podcast.body: World Party's debut album, "Private Revolution," featured significant alt-rock songs that integrated influences from legendary artists. "The debut album entitled Private Revolution featured some great alt rock songs that channeled influences of the Beatles, Bob Dylan, the Beach Boys, the Stones, Prince and Van Morrison."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
